title: First Fix
summary: Recover from a deliberately poor initial orbit estimate. Watch prediction and correction trade places.

briefing.markdown:
**Situation.** A 550 km, 51.6° spacecraft has just separated from its launcher. The launch provider's state vector is off by about **2.7 km in position and 2.7 m/s in velocity** — and our filter knows it is uncertain at that level ($\sigma = 2$ km, $2$ m/s per axis).

**Your tools.** A GNSS receiver delivers a position fix every 10 s with $\sigma = 5$ m. An **Extended Kalman Filter** combines those fixes with two-body physics,
$$\ddot{\mathbf r} = -\frac{\mu}{r^3}\mathbf r .$$

**What to watch.** In the 3-D view the **teal** track is truth and the **amber** marker is the estimate, wrapped in its uncertainty ellipsoid (magnified). Step the **Predict** and **Update** phases separately at least once: the ellipsoid swells during prediction and collapses at each fix.

prediction.prompt: The first GNSS fix arrives at $t = 0$ with $\sigma = 5$ m. Right after it, roughly how large is the **velocity** uncertainty?

options.text: About 5 m/s — the fix is only good to 5 m.
options.feedback: The fix doesn't measure velocity at all. Its 5 m precision limits *position*.

options.text: Still about 2 m/s — one position fix says nothing about velocity.
options.feedback: Exactly. A single position sample carries no velocity information; the observability check confirms rank 3 at a single instant. It takes a *sequence* of fixes to pin down velocity.

options.text: Close to zero — the filter now knows everything.
options.feedback: Only the three position components are pinned down. Velocity needs a second fix (and a model connecting the two).

prediction.explanation: Velocity becomes observable only through the dynamics: $\mathbf r(t_2) \approx \mathbf r(t_1) + \mathbf v\,\Delta t$. Watch the velocity σ fall after the *second* fix.

interactive.instructions: Press **Play**, or step node by node. Try **Predict** then **Update** to see one full filter cycle. Open the *Uncertainty* and *Errors* plots.
steps: Step one **Predict** and one **Update** — watch the ellipsoid.
Play until the position σ drops below 10 m.
Run the **observability check** with a 0 s window, then 60 s. Compare the rank.

objectives.text: Step through one Predict → Update cycle
Bring the 1σ position uncertainty below 10 m
Fly to the end of the pass (3000 s)

hints.text: The **P** and **U** keys step the predict and update phases separately.
Velocity uncertainty drops only after the *second* fix — check the *States* plot for vx.

actions.text: See the ellipsoid snap smaller? That's $P^+ = (I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^\top + KRK^\top$ at work. The **position** collapsed; velocity barely moved — yet.
Position uncertainty under 10 m — from 3.5 km at launch. The filter now trusts its own predictions about as much as each new fix.

reasoning.prompt: After a few minutes the filter's position σ settles near 1–2 m, **smaller** than the 5 m GNSS noise. How can the estimate be better than any single measurement?

options.text: It can't — the plot must be wrong.
options.feedback: It can, and it is right: the NEES check in the debrief confirms the error really is that small.

options.text: The filter averages many fixes through the dynamics model, so independent noise partly cancels.
options.feedback: Yes. Each fix adds information; the dynamics model ties them together, so the posterior is tighter than any one measurement — as long as the model is good.

options.text: GNSS secretly gets more accurate over time.
options.feedback: The true noise stays at 5 m throughout. The improvement comes from combining measurements.

scoring.successMessage: Orbit determined. Hand-over to routine operations.

debrief.markdown:
**What happened.** The first fix pinned position but left velocity at its launch uncertainty. Each later fix, combined with the dynamics, revealed velocity: the **observability** of velocity comes from the *sequence* of positions, not from any single one.

**The numbers.** The steady-state position error sits below the 5 m measurement noise because the filter averages many measurements through the model. The calibration score checks that the filter's *claimed* uncertainty matched its *actual* error (ANEES/n ≈ 1).

**Take-away.** $K$ is large when the prediction is poor and small when it is good. That is why the first update moved the estimate by kilometres and later ones by centimetres.
